doc.title: David Finck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 29, 2015

title: Philosophy of the bassist's role: rhythm and voice leading
summary: Finck explains the bass function as rhythm plus voice leading from Bach, admires Ron Carter and Paul Chambers, and agrees the bass drives a band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: As a bassist in a jazz group, or frankly as a bassist in any group, there is a lot of function in your job description. You have to function rhythmically and you have to function harmonically. And I’ve discovered after all these years and after having listened to hundreds of other bassists, that there are limited numbers of ways of effectively guiding a band through the harmony of the song and the bass lines that we construct in the moment have to function to help shape the harmony. In other words, if we’ve all agreed that we’re going to play “Happy Birthday” in the key of F, and the pianist or guitarist or another harmonic instrument, although it’s not required, once we agree on the chord changes, that I have to function in a way in which I create the bottom of that harmony, which is the bass, the foundation for it. And that in working my way to the next chord in a song, I have to effectively guide everybody so they know where we’re going. The pianist has to do it too, but I can do it without the pianist, and he can do it without me (he or she). So my philosophy is basically one of rhythm and I guess you would call it basic voice leading, which comes from Bach essentially. Those little Bach chorales that we had to learn in music school, those bass lines are unbelievable. And when I listen to my favorite bass players, whether they know it or not, that’s what they’re doing. So I’m particularly

fond of Ron Carter’s bass lines. When Ron Carter walks a bass line I can often hear the implied harmony between the major resting places in a song. It’s like, oh yeah that would be a diminished chord and that would be a dominant chord, and that gets me to the next place. It’s all in there. Paul Chambers also.
Because you can mess up two things at once, right?
Yes. Well we all can. I’m good at messing up all kinds of things. But yes, you know, really good bass players in many ways drive a band more than a drummer in many ways.

I concur. Because you think of some of the famous trios with guitar, piano and bass — hardly any with piano, drums and reed instrument or something like that. I mean the bass is more to be missed when it’s not there.
I would agree, and that keeps us employed.
